# Type 2 diabetes

> *When insulin resistance outpaces what the pancreas can compensate for, blood glucose rises, and type 2
> diabetes is diagnosed once it stays high. We cover that progression, dietary management (starting
> with safety alongside glucose-lowering drugs, then carbohydrate quality and dietary patterns),
> remission and prevention, and when to refer.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how insulin resistance progresses to type 2 diabetes through β-cell compensation and failure,
  and how liver and pancreatic fat sustain it in the twin-cycle model.
- Explain why carbohydrate quality and consistency, not a fixed carbohydrate target, guide the diet, and
  translate them into wholegrain and sugary-drink swaps at a hawker stall.
- Recognise a realistic candidate for remission of early type 2 diabetes, explain why remission is not
  cure, and refer to a supervised programme.
- Explain why a structured lifestyle programme prevents progression from prediabetes where one-off
  advice does not, and refer to one.
- Identify the glucose-lowering drug classes that can cause hypoglycaemia, and refer for a medication review
  before endorsing a low-carbohydrate diet or a fast.
- Recognise the risks of Ramadan fasting with diabetes, address the belief that a finger-prick test
  breaks the fast, and refer for a pre-Ramadan review.
:::

## Type 2 diabetes at a glance {#sec-overview}

Type 2 diabetes develops from insulin resistance, the reduced response of the body's cells to insulin
(see the *Obesity & metabolic syndrome* chapter). Nutrition matters throughout the course of the
disease. It prevents progression in people with **prediabetes**, the phase in which blood glucose has
started to rise but is not yet in the diabetes range. It manages established diabetes, and it can put
early disease into **remission**, with blood glucose held below the diabetes range off
glucose-lowering drugs (see [Remission](#sec-t2d-remission)).

![The diabetes continuum and where nutrition acts: from at-risk, through prediabetes, to early and then established type 2 diabetes. Structured lifestyle change can prevent progression; a supervised, weight-centred programme can put *early* disease into remission; dietary quality manages established disease; medication (a specialist decision) is layered on, not a substitute.](/figures/mechanisms/t2d-continuum.svg){#fig-t2d-continuum width="92%" fig-align="center"}

The complications of type 2 diabetes in the heart, blood vessels and kidneys are taught in the
*Cardiovascular disease & hypertension* and *Chronic kidney disease* chapters. Gestational diabetes,
and why Singapore screens every pregnancy, is in the *Pregnancy & lactation* chapter.

Safety comes before any diet advice. Before endorsing a low-carbohydrate diet or a fast, you need to
know which glucose-lowering drugs the patient takes. Some cause dangerous hypoglycaemia (blood glucose
falling too low; see the *Integrative metabolism* chapter) when carbohydrate is cut.

All of this is part of Singapore's War on Diabetes: roughly one in three people will develop
diabetes in their lifetime [@mohWarOnDiabetes].

## Pathophysiology: how insulin resistance becomes diabetes {#sec-t2d-mechanism}

Type 2 diabetes is the end result of a long period of compensation for insulin resistance by the pancreatic **β-cells**
(the insulin-producing cells; insulin action and glucose handling are in the *Integrative metabolism*
chapter). The progression has four steps:

::: {.flow}
[From insulin resistance to raised glucose]{.tree-title}

1. Insulin resistance
2. β-cells compensate
3. Insulin secretion declines
4. Blood glucose rises
:::

For years, β-cell compensation offsets insulin resistance. When tissues respond less to insulin, the
β-cells secrete more of it, which keeps blood glucose normal. Diabetes appears when the β-cells can
no longer keep up: insulin secretion declines progressively on top of the resistance
[@ada2026standards]. Diabetes is therefore usually preceded by a long, silent prediabetes phase, and
that phase is the window for early detection.

The **twin-cycle model** offers one explanation of why the β-cells fail. Excess fat in the liver
drives up fasting glucose (the liver cycle), while fat in the pancreas impairs the β-cells' ability to
respond (the pancreas cycle), and each cycle reinforces the other [@taylor2021remission;
@taylor2025twincycle]. This organ fat is ectopic fat (fat stored in organs where it does not belong;
see the *Obesity & metabolic syndrome* chapter), and it is removable. Substantial weight loss removes
it, which can restore β-cell function and reverse early disease. That reversal is the basis of
remission (see [Remission](#sec-t2d-remission)).

Asians carry more fat at a given BMI (see the *Obesity & metabolic syndrome* chapter). Each person has
a **personal fat threshold**, the individual level of body fat beyond which diabetes develops. An Asian
patient can therefore cross it at a BMI below the Western cut-offs [@taylor2023pft].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient has had insulin resistance for years, yet his blood glucose was normal until recently. Why?
His β-cells compensated by secreting more insulin, which kept blood glucose normal for years. Glucose
rises only when β-cell insulin secretion declines and can no longer keep up with the resistance. That
is why type 2 diabetes is usually preceded by a long, silent prediabetes phase.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can substantial weight loss reverse early type 2 diabetes?
In the twin-cycle model, fat in the liver raises fasting glucose and fat in the pancreas impairs the
β-cells, and each cycle reinforces the other. This ectopic fat is removable: substantial weight loss removes
it and can restore β-cell function, which is the basis of remission in early disease.
:::

## Dietary management: medication safety, carbohydrate and dietary pattern {#sec-t2d-levers}

### Safety before any diet change {#sec-t2d-safety}

#### Hypoglycaemia risk by drug class {#sec-t2d-hypoglycaemia}

Cutting or skipping carbohydrate, or fasting, is only safe once you know the patient's medication,
because a few glucose-lowering drug classes can cause dangerous hypoglycaemia. The first step, every
time, is therefore to identify the drug class and the action that follows from it [@ada2026glycemic;
@aceT2DM2023]:

| Hypoglycaemia risk | Drug classes | Action before cutting carbohydrate |
|---|---|---|
| High | insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides | Risk of dangerous hypoglycaemia: refer to the diabetes team to review medication first |
| Low when used alone | metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists | A sensible carbohydrate-quality change is reasonable; still refer to a dietitian |

Older people on sulfonylureas or insulin are especially vulnerable to hypoglycaemia
[@ling2021elderlyhypo]. One further caution is unrelated to hypoglycaemia: on an SGLT2 inhibitor, a very-low-carbohydrate
or ketogenic diet should be avoided, because the combination can trigger diabetic ketoacidosis
[@ada2026standards].

Select a patient's medications in the interactive below to see whether a low-carbohydrate plan is safe
to endorse or needs the diabetes team first.

<div data-island="carb-safety-check" data-src="/diagrams/carb-safety-check.yml"></div>

For someone on a fixed insulin dose, the counselling message is **carbohydrate consistency** (steady
timing and amount of carbohydrate from day to day), not aggressive restriction.

Hypoglycaemia in a conscious patient is treated with the **15-15 rule** (about 15 g of fast-acting
glucose, then a recheck in 15 minutes), not with chocolate or nuts, whose fat slows absorption
[@diabetesukHypo].

#### Fasting for Ramadan with diabetes {#sec-t2d-ramadan}

For Singapore's Malay-Muslim community, which also carries a high diabetes burden, Ramadan fasting is
an important, faith-sensitive counselling topic (the fed–fasted physiology of Ramadan is in the
*Integrative metabolism* chapter). Most Muslim patients with diabetes fast, and in a 13-country survey
severe hypoglycaemia was several times more frequent during Ramadan than in other months
[@salti2004epidiar]. The danger is greatest for patients on insulin or a sulfonylurea, two of the
high-risk classes in the table above.

Many patients believe that a finger-prick glucose test breaks the fast, and some come to harm because
of that belief [@zainudin2017knowledge]. The test does not break the fast, and Islam exempts the
medically unfit, so monitoring and, where needed, not fasting are religiously permissible.

### Carbohydrate: quality and consistency {#sec-t2d-carbohydrate}

Carbohydrate is the dietary component that most directly raises blood glucose after a meal, so it is
the natural focus. Yet there is no mandated carbohydrate target and no single ideal macronutrient
ratio for diabetes [@ada2026standards; @dyson2018diabetesuk]. What matters is carbohydrate quality and
day-to-day consistency, individualised by a dietitian, not a number set at the bedside.

Carbohydrate quality matters more than quantity. Choosing lower-glycaemic, wholegrain, higher-fibre
carbohydrates gives a small but real improvement in blood glucose: about 0.3% off **HbA1c**, a blood
marker of average blood glucose over about three months [@chiavaroli2021gigl]. That improvement is
best achieved through specific food swaps, not by memorising glycaemic-index tables (see the *Macronutrients*
chapter), which are measured for single foods and blunted in mixed meals [@dnsg2023easd].

Fibre and wholegrains have the strongest, most consistent evidence. Higher intake lowers the risk of
developing diabetes; across a range of outcomes in the general population, the risk reduction was
greatest at around 25–29 g of fibre a day [@reynolds2019carbquality]. In established disease it lowers
HbA1c, and raising intake by about 15 g a day, or to about 35 g, is a reasonable target
[@reynolds2020fibrediabetes]. International guidelines give the
same advice: carbohydrate mainly from wholegrains, vegetables, fruit and legumes, with refined grains
and sugary drinks kept to a minimum [@who2023carbohydrate].

![Swapping toward wholegrains (brown rice for white, wholemeal for white bread) is a key carbohydrate-quality change; locally it is a swap, not a ban on rice.](/figures/food/brown-rice.jpg){#fig-brown-rice width="55%" fig-align="center"}

Sugar-sweetened drinks are a separate, important target. Each daily serving is associated with
roughly a 13–18% higher risk of type 2 diabetes, an effect only partly explained by weight
[@imamura2015ssb]. Singapore's Nutri-Grade label works as a decision aid here [@shin2023nutrigrade].
Ordering *kopi kosong* or *teh kosong* (no sugar), or *kopi* or *teh siu dai* (less sweet), is an
intervention in its own right.

::: {.callout-important}
## Should a patient with diabetes give up rice?
Rice is often blamed for diabetes, and pooled Asian data do link white rice to diabetes risk
[@hu2012whiterice]. In the Singapore Chinese Health Study, however, rice intake itself was not
associated with diabetes, while substituting wholemeal bread lowered risk [@seah2019scriphealthrice].
The accurate, less stigmatising message is to shift toward wholegrains (and add vegetables and protein
to the plate) instead of demonising a cultural staple. Wholegrain intake is still low locally: only about 4%
of the staples Singaporeans eat are wholegrain [@mohNNS2022].
:::

### Choosing a dietary pattern {#sec-t2d-patterns}

Because quality matters more than the macronutrient ratio, several dietary patterns are acceptable,
and the right one is the one a person will actually follow [@evert2019nutrition]. The evidence behind
three common patterns (see the *What a healthy diet looks like* chapter) differs:

- The Mediterranean pattern has the strongest diabetes-specific evidence. It lowers HbA1c in established
  disease, reduces new cases, and works well translated into local food instead of adopted wholesale
  [@esposito2015medjourney; @koloverou2014medincidence].
- A low-carbohydrate pattern is a legitimate option. Its benefit at six months tends to attenuate
  by twelve and depends heavily on adherence, and strict versions need dietitian supervision
  [@goldenberg2021lowcarb].
- A DASH-style pattern also helps glucose [@fang2025dash4d], although there are still too few
  diabetes-specific DASH trials to rank it confidently [@jing2023networkma].

The cardiovascular evidence for the Mediterranean and DASH patterns (PREDIMED, and DASH's
blood-pressure and lipid rationale) is in the *Cardiovascular disease & hypertension* chapter. In
diabetes, these patterns matter for glucose and overall diet quality.

The **plate method**, a tool that sets the proportions of the plate without counting, lets any of these
patterns be applied at a *cai png* (mixed-rice) stall. Singapore's version, My Healthy Plate, is a quarter
wholegrains, a quarter protein and half fruit and vegetables, with water over sugary drinks
[@hpbHealthyPlate].

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
At the *cai png* stall the advice is concrete: less rice (or brown rice), one lean protein, two
vegetables, and go easy on the gravy. At the drinks stall, choose *kopi-o kosong*, *teh-o kosong* or
water over a Nutri-Grade C/D sweet drink. This is the Mediterranean and plate-method principle (more
plants and wholegrains, less refined carbohydrate and sugar) in hawker-centre terms.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why is the advice to swap toward brown rice, instead of cutting rice out or setting a carbohydrate target?
There is no mandated carbohydrate target; what matters is carbohydrate quality and consistency, and
the strongest evidence is for fibre and wholegrains. In the Singapore Chinese Health Study, rice intake itself was not associated with diabetes, while substituting wholemeal bread lowered
risk. A swap toward wholegrains is accurate, keeps a cultural staple on the plate and avoids stigma.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a low-carbohydrate diet improved a patient's glucose at six months. Does that make it his best long-term pattern?
Not necessarily. The low-carbohydrate benefit tends to attenuate by twelve months and depends heavily
on adherence, and several quality patterns are acceptable. The right pattern is the one he will follow,
and a strict version needs dietitian supervision.
:::

## Remission and prevention {#sec-t2d-remission-prevention}

### Remission of early type 2 diabetes {#sec-t2d-remission}

Early type 2 diabetes can be put into remission with substantial, sustained weight loss. The landmark
DiRECT trial (Diabetes Remission Clinical Trial) achieved 46% remission at one year with a structured
weight-management programme, versus 4% with usual care [@lean2018direct]. Three qualifiers must
accompany that number:

- It applies to eligible patients only. DiRECT enrolled people diagnosed within about 6 years,
  not on insulin, within a defined BMI range. Long-standing or insulin-treated diabetes behaves
  differently. Because Asians reach their personal fat threshold at a lower BMI, entry criteria
  should be ethnicity-adjusted rather than the Western band applied unchanged [@taylor2023pft;
  @standby2022southasian].
- It fades over time. Remission fell to about 36% at two years and about 13% at five,
  in line with weight regain; the maintenance problem is not yet solved [@direct5yr2024].
- It is remission, not cure. The agreed definition is an HbA1c below the diabetes range sustained off
  glucose-lowering drugs, and monitoring continues because it can relapse [@riddle2021remission;
  @diabetesUK2021remission].

How a remission programme is delivered matters for safety. Programmes use a supervised **total diet
replacement**: a low-calorie formula phase with structured food reintroduction. The programme's
clinical team adjusts the medication on day one, because glucose and blood pressure fall fast. A total
diet replacement is therefore not a self-directed crash diet: the referring clinician's task is to
recognise the candidate and refer to a structured programme. Singapore has an expert-consensus
framework for this (with ethnicity-adjusted thresholds), though no national remission programme yet
exists [@khoo2026sgDSF].

### Preventing diabetes: structured lifestyle programmes {#sec-t2d-prevention}

Prevention acts before diagnosis, and how it is delivered determines whether it works. In the
Diabetes Prevention Program, an intensive, structured lifestyle programme cut progression from
prediabetes to diabetes by 58% relative to placebo (from about 11 to about 5 new cases per 100 people a
year), outperforming metformin (31%, about 8 per 100) [@dpp2002]. The benefit persists for
decades, even as it attenuates [@dppos2009; @dppos2025_21yr]. What made the programme effective was its
structure: a multi-session curriculum with follow-up, aiming at ≥7% weight loss and ≥150 minutes of
activity a week. A one-off "you should lose weight" has none of that structure. Translated at scale it
still works: the NHS programme and, locally, the Pre-DICTED trial reproduced the benefit in real-world
and multi-ethnic Asian settings [@mcmanus2022nhsDpp; @bee2025predicted].

The guideline advice for prediabetes has three parts: aim for modest weight loss and activity, adopt a
quality dietary pattern, and refer to a structured programme [@ada2026prevention]. When you discuss
prediabetes, frame it to motivate, not to frighten, since not everyone with prediabetes progresses,
and some revert to normal [@hpbPreDictedInfo]. Sustaining any of these changes is a skill in itself
(see the *Behaviour-change counselling* chapter for motivational interviewing and other
behaviour-change techniques).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why should remission programmes in Singapore use ethnicity-adjusted entry criteria instead of DiRECT's Western BMI band?
Asians carry more fat at a given BMI, so they can cross their personal fat threshold into diabetes at
a BMI below the Western cut-offs. A BMI band set on Western populations therefore underestimates
how much body fat an Asian patient carries at a given weight. Singapore's expert-consensus framework
uses ethnicity-adjusted thresholds.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient with prediabetes was told once, at a clinic visit, to lose some weight. Why is that unlikely to reproduce the Diabetes Prevention Program result?
What made the Diabetes Prevention Program effective was its structure: a multi-session curriculum
with follow-up, aiming at a weight loss of at least 7% and at least 150 minutes of activity a week. A one-off
conversation has none of that structure. The guideline response is to refer to a structured programme.
:::

## When to refer {#sec-t2d-refer}

The clinician's task is to recognise and refer, not to prescribe. You identify the modifiable dietary
factors: carbohydrate quality, dietary pattern, body weight (for remission) and sugary-drink intake. You
then refer to a dietitian for the individualised plan (medical nutrition therapy; see the
*Interprofessional practice, referral and looking after yourself* chapter) and to the diabetes team for medication decisions.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Review the medication before carbohydrate is cut
It is unsafe to endorse a low-carbohydrate diet or a fast to a patient on insulin or a sulfonylurea
without a medication review. The dose set for their old intake can now drive their blood glucose too
low. Recognise the risk, and refer to the diabetes team **before** the diet changes, not after.
:::

Ramadan fasting needs the same medication review, made in advance.

The safe approach is a **pre-Ramadan review**: a consultation, ideally weeks ahead, to risk-stratify
the patient and adjust medication, following international guidance [@hassanein2022ramadan]. It is a
recognise-and-refer task, not one to manage single-handed. Singapore's locally validated fasting
algorithm (the FAST algorithm; see the *Integrative metabolism* chapter) shows that fasting with
diabetes can be done safely when medication is adjusted by the algorithm [@lum2020fast].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: two patients want to try a low-carbohydrate diet, one on metformin alone and one on a sulfonylurea. Why does only one need a medication review first?
Sulfonylureas, like insulin and meglitinides, can cause hypoglycaemia: the dose set for the patient's
usual intake can drive glucose too low once carbohydrate is cut. Metformin used alone carries a low
hypoglycaemia risk, so a sensible carbohydrate-quality change is reasonable, with a dietitian
referral. The patient on the sulfonylurea needs the diabetes team to review the medication before the
diet changes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient on insulin plans to fast for Ramadan and will not test her glucose, because she believes a finger-prick breaks the fast. What follows?
Severe hypoglycaemia is several times more frequent during Ramadan, insulin is one of the drugs that can
cause it, and her belief removes the monitoring that would catch it. A finger-prick test does not break the fast, and Islam exempts the
medically unfit, so monitoring is religiously permissible. The task is to address the belief and refer
for a pre-Ramadan review to risk-stratify her and adjust medication.
:::

## Can diabetes be "reversed"? {#sec-close}

Sometimes. A supervised, weight-centred programme that removes ectopic fat from the liver and pancreas
can put early type 2 diabetes into remission. Remission is not cure: the benefit is real but limited to
eligible patients, and it can fade as weight returns. For most people, the gains come from
prevention and day-to-day management: structured lifestyle change prevents progression from
prediabetes, and a quality carbohydrate pattern with the plate method manages established disease. The
individualised plan is made by referral, to the dietitian and the diabetes team.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Singapore declared a War on Diabetes in 2016. About one in three Singaporeans will develop diabetes in
their lifetime [@mohWarOnDiabetes], and current prevalence is around 9% of adults [@mohNPHS2024].
Prevalence has an ethnic gradient: Indian and Malay residents have roughly twice the prevalence of
Chinese residents [@mohNPHS2024]. The gradient should guide screening priority, framed as
population-level risk and never as blame; counselling is still tailored to the individual.

These modifiable dietary factors are prominent in the local food environment: only ~4% of
staples are wholegrain, and sugary drinks supply about half of dietary sugar [@mohNNS2022]. The
national tools target these same factors: My Healthy Plate, Nutri-Grade on beverages
[@mohNutriGradeFresh2023], and Healthier SG, with its subsidised screening, as the main route to
early detection and lifestyle advice [@mohHealthierSG; @mohHealthierSGScreening].

On medication, local guidance from the Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE) names the classes: metformin
first-line, and SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists where heart or kidney risk warrants
[@aceT2DM2023]. The task at this stage is to know that these tiers exist and that prescribing is the
diabetes team's job.
